newsitem.title: INDIA: India, U.S. talk big on trade, but barriers seen.
newsitem.headline: India, U.S. talk big on trade, but barriers seen.

text.p: India and the United States see major opportunities to boost business, but there are major irritants in the form of barriers in key trade areas on both sides, analysts said on Wednesday.

U.S. defence authorities have identified India as a strategically important nation based on economic considerations, Professor V. Ramachandriah of the state-funded Indian Institute of Foreign Trade (IIFT) told Reuters in New Delhi.
Ramachandriah said President Bill Clinton had India in mind along with East Asian economies when he mentioned trade with Asia as a priority area in his State of the Union speech on Tuesday.

"Now we must act to expand our exports, especially to Asia and Latin America, two of the fastest growing regions on earth -- or be left behind as these emerging economies forge new ties with other nations," Clinton said.

The United States accounts for around 70 percent of the $5.0 billion in foreign investments India has approved since 1991, Ramachandriah said. "The U.S. is the largest investor in India after liberalisation," he said.

Washington expected India to be a major regional economic power based on its economic reforms since 1991, its huge pool of scientific and educational human resources and its 930 million people, Ramachandriah said.
The United States had an edge in areas like power, telecommunications, port and highway development in which India was seeking huge amounts of foreign investment, he said.
U.S.-based Enron Corp became a pioneering investor in the Indian power sector.
U.S. firms also had an edge in selling computers, aircraft and electronic instruments and machinery, Ramachandriah said.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda met Microsoft Corp's chairman Bill Gates at Davos in Switzerland this week. Indian newspapers have said Gates plans an Indian joint venture in computer software.
"Bill Gates wants to be here in a big way," said P.L. Sanjeeva Reddy, IIFT's director-general.
The United States has been India's biggest trading partner, even during the Cold War years when New Delhi's Soviet links generated huge volumes of rupee-based trade.
Washington accounted for $5.5 billion, or 17.2 percent, of Indian exports worth $31.8 billion in 1995/96 (April-March) and $3.8 billion, or 10.4 percent, of imports worth $36.4 billion.
But Indian analysts say there are still many irritants that make business far from smooth.
In 1989, Washington threatened to slap trade sanctions on India for not opening up its insurance sector, and in 1991 for not amending its patent laws.
Indian insisted on discussing both issues at the Uruguay Round of world trade talks. "These were unilateral actions. They have been acting as irritants," Ramachandriah said.
India has set regulatory steps to open up its insurance sector, but is yet to allow foreign investment.
The World Trade Organisation, the Geneva-based global trade watchdog, has given India a decade to amend its patent laws to conform with international standards.
The U.S. was also trying to impose trade curbs on environmental grounds, and was delaying the opening up of its textile markets, Ramachandriah said.
